Original learning chapter · updated 9 September 2026. Equations and examples explain concepts; they are not test acceptance or a support matrix.

Prerequisites: 05 · Barycentric coordinates and interpolation, 06 · Cameras, projection and reconstructing depth

A pixel asks which surfaces cover it

Rasterization converts projected triangles into samples on an image grid. It is not yet lighting: a fragment can contain a face ID, barycentric weights and depth without containing a final color. Keeping these stages separate makes it possible to inspect whether a wrong image came from projection, coverage, interpolation, texture lookup or shading.

For a chosen pixel sample, signed edge functions classify which side of each triangle edge contains the sample. With consistent orientation, the signs determine whether it lies inside. Shared edges need a consistent ownership convention so two adjacent triangles neither leave cracks nor accidentally double-count the same boundary sample. Floating-point precision and degenerate projected triangles make these details part of the implementation contract.

Worked example

For the triangle (0,0),(2,0),(0,2), the sample (0.5,0.5) has weights (0.5,0.25,0.25), so it lies inside. The sample (1.5,1.5) is outside because x+y exceeds two. If another triangle covers the first sample, depth determines which fragment is nearer. A top-K representation retains several candidates instead of assuming there can be only one surface per pixel.

Where differentiability becomes conditional

Within a fixed face assignment, barycentric coordinates and interpolated depth can vary smoothly with vertex positions. At a silhouette or a depth-order swap, the selected face changes discretely. Differentiating the continuous arithmetic while holding that selection fixed does not provide the missing visibility derivative. A finite-difference check that crosses a boundary is probing a different mathematical question from a local derivative check inside one region.

Aliasing is a sampling problem: one pixel-centre sample cannot represent every tiny feature. Supersampling and filtering can reduce it, but do not automatically make visibility differentiable. Likewise, a signed distance output is useful evidence about coverage but is not itself a physically meaningful transparency model.

Try it yourself

Can correct barycentric interpolation guarantee a correct silhouette?

Answer

No. Interpolation only acts after coverage and face selection. An incorrect edge rule or missing triangle can leave the weights correct for the wrong selected surface.

gffx boundary

The current rasterizer returns face indices, barycentrics, depths and signed distances. Its signed-distance quantity uses squared pixel units and is negative inside; treating it as linear distance changes softness parameters. Background slots, sorting and local gradients are defined by operation tests. This is not the future complete deferred renderer, path tracer or a claim of differentiable occlusion.

From a test head to a reference image

A reference image is a measuring stick, not necessarily a photograph or a beautiful render. The synthetic head fixture keeps its geometry, camera, light and four colour sources fixed. For each covered pixel, divide the screen-space barycentric weights by the three corner view depths and renormalize. Those corrected weights interpolate world position, smooth normal, UV coordinates and vertex colour. Normalizing the interpolated normal restores a unit direction. Reprojecting the reconstructed world point must recover that same pixel centre: this independently catches many coordinate and interpolation mistakes.

The first row of the sixteen-panel demonstration shows colour before lighting. The next two rows show independently evaluated diffuse and classic directional lighting. The last row is an exact diffuse-only control: uniform unit incident radiance over the hemisphere returns the surface albedo when the view is on the positive side. Eight actual head pixels are also checked with independent hemisphere quadrature. This is not full environment integration for every material or pixel.

Reference and future candidate shading deliberately share geometry buffers. Consequently, their agreement can establish a lighting equation without proving the rasterizer itself correct. Keep independent projection and texture controls alongside the image test. Compare raw linear float64 RGB only on an explicit coverage mask; count both pixels and channels and require zero background. A different mask, swapped colour channels or brighter light must fail. The enlarged sRGB preview is for people, not the numerical comparison. Hashes protect stored bytes and provenance but cannot make a wrong mathematical answer right.
